Did Moses go to Heaven in the Bible? If not, why didn't he go to Heaven? WHO GOES TO HEAVEN? by Michael R. Burch Did Moses go to heaven? Yes, no, maybe and it depends. It depends on which author of the Bible one reads. Since many Christians claim that Moses wrote the Pentateuch (the first five books of the Old Testament), let’s start with Moses himself and work our way forward. But I have to warn you — it’s going to be a rollercoaster ride, so hold onto your hats! I will give each book one vote. Moses never said a word about heaven, hell or the Devil. If Moses wrote the first five books of the Old Testament, his verdict is clear: The penalty for sin was death. Human beings went to Sheol when they died, not “hell” as Sheol was incorrectly translated in the error-riddled King Jame Version (KJV) of the Bible. There was no heaven, no hell, and no Devil. It bears noting that the Sadducees denied there would be a resurrection because it wasn’t taught in the Pentateuch. [FIVE BOOKS: NO=5, YES=0, MAYBE=0] The next 12 books of the Bible never mention heaven, hell or the Devil, to my recollection: Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther. [17 BOOKS: NO=17, YES=0, MAYBE=0] Job is generally thought to be one of the older books of the Old Testament, so this may be the oldest verse that mentions a resurrection: I know that my redeemer lives, and that in the end he will stand on the earth. And after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God; I myself will see him with my own eyes—I, and not another. How my heart yearns within me! (Job 19:25-27) But why didn’t the great Moses known anything about any of this? [18 BOOKS: NO=17, YES=1, MAYBE=0] Psalms I have set the LORD always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken. Therefore my heart is glad, and my whole being rejoices; my flesh also dwells secure. For you will not abandon my soul to Sheol [the grave, not hell] or let your holy one see corruption. You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore. (Psalm 16:8-11) This verse is a bit dicey because its says “your holy one” and who knows what that means? Also the “holy one” will not see “corruption” but our bodies decompose in the grave. Christians often claim this verse is about Jesus. But this doesn’t seem to apply to Moses, or us, so I will count this as a “maybe.” This is the path of those who have foolish confidence; yet after them people approve of their boasts. Like sheep they are appointed for Sheol [the grave, not hell]; death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning. Their form shall be consumed in Sheol, with no place to dwell. But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me. Again, it’s hard to say who will be saved here. Another “maybe.” You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again. Again, it’s hard to say why one person is receiving what seems to be special treatment. Would this apply to Moses, or to us? Another “maybe.” [19 BOOKS: NO=17, YES=1, MAYBE=1] After 19 books we don’t have much to go on. Proverbs Ecclesiastes According to the book itself, it was written not only by the Bible’s wisest man, but the wisest man who would ever life. And the wisest man of all makes it very clear that the is no afterlife, and that man has no preeminence over beasts because their end is the same. (Entire book) [21 BOOKS: NO=19, YES=1, MAYBE=1] Song of Songs Isaiah He will swallow up death for all time, And the Lord GOD will wipe tears away from all faces. (Isaiah 25:8) Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! For your dew is a dew of light, and the earth will give birth to the dead. and the earth will give birth to the dead. Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by. (Isaiah 26:19-20) This sounds like a universal resurrection to me. It is possible that both passages above are talking about Israel as a nation overcoming its enemies. The part about hiding to avoid the fury (of war?) seems of this earth. But I will count Isaiah as a “yes.” [23 BOOKS: NO=20, YES=2, MAYBE=1] Yet it was the will of the LORD to crush him; he has put him to grief; when his soul makes an offering for guilt, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days; the will of the LORD shall prosper in his hand. Out of the anguish of his soul he shall see [light] and be satisfied; by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities. This verse is treated as a prophecy about Jesus but it says “he shall prolong his days” and Jesus died young. I see nothing here about a resurrection. (Isaiah 53:11-10) Jeremiah Lamentations Ezekiel So I prophesied as I was commanded. And as I prophesied, there was a sound, and behold, a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to its bone. And I looked, and behold, there were sinews on them, and flesh had come upon them, and skin had covered them. But there was no breath in them. Then he said to me, “Prophesy to the breath; prophesy, son of man, and say to the breath, Thus says the Lord God: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live.” So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived and stood on their feet, an exceedingly great army. (Ezekiel 37:7–10) This is the famous “Valley of Dry Bones” vision of the prophet Ezekiel. This seems to be about a universal resurrection, entirely by the power of God, with no human faith required. However, here death could be a metaphor for Israelites living in exile, and life a metaphor for a return to the Promised Land. But I will count it as a “yes.” [26 BOOKS: NO=22, YES=3, MAYBE=1] Daniel And many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever. (Daniel 12:2-3) Here we see “many” being resurrected but not all, and the first mention of negative consequences for some. I will count this as a “yes” but the author of Daniel seems to be in disagreement with the other yeses so far. It should be noted that Daniel was influenced by the Babylonian captivity — for instance the introduction of the archangels Michael and Gabriel. [27 BOOKS: NO=22, YES=4, MAYBE=1] Hosea Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up. After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him. (Hosea 6:1-2) I see nothing about a resurrection here. It sounds more like something happening here on earth. We have to “return” to the LORD, which we can’t do once in the grave. This is a “maybe” for me. Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol? Shall I redeem them from death? O Death, where are your thorns? O Sheol, where is your sting? (Hosea 13:14) This sounds like a resurrection verse to me. [28 BOOKS: NO=22, YES=5, MAYBE=1] Joel Amos Obadiah Jonah And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights. . . . Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish, saying, “I called out to the LORD, out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice. . . . I went down to the land whose bars closed upon me forever; yet you brought up my life from the pit, O LORD my God. When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple.” . . . And the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land. Jonah was in the belly of a Leviathan and compared it to being in Sheol (the grave). The Leviathan spat him out. I see no resurrection here. Not even a “maybe.” Micah Nahum Habakkuk Zephaniah Haggai Zechariah Malachi [39 BOOKS: NO=33, YES=5, MAYBE=1] That’s not exactly a ringing endorsement for a resurrection, with the greatest Hebrew prophet Moses saying nothing on the subject and with the few possibly affirmative verses being possibly about Israel as a nation rather than individuals. NEW TESTAMENT FOLLIES When we get to the New Testament things remain dicey because the authors had a tendency cite prophecies that can’t be found as cited in the Old Testament, and to create deceptive stories to make prophecies seem to have been “fulfilled” about Jesus. As I have been known to ask, “Can a true religion be based on lies?” Here are some quick examples: In 1 Corinthians 15:3-5 the apostle Paul, or someone pretending to be Paul, says: “3 For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, 4 that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, 5 and that he appeared to Cephas, and then to the Twelve. 6 After that, he appeared to more than five hundred of the brothers and sisters at the same time, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep.” There are quite a few problems here: As for making up BS in order to make it seem that Jesus fulfilled Old Testament prophecies, take the nonsense about Joseph having to go to Bethlehem because of a census. That was clear fraud. If Herod the Great was alive when Jesus was born, as the Bible claims, he died in 4 BC, and that’s 10 years before the census cited. The census of Quirinius was taken long after Herod’s death, so the authors of the New Testament were lying and unable to keep their lies straight. Furthermore, the Romans counted and taxed people where they lived, and never required them to return to their places of birth. Why the deception? Because Jesus was called Jesus of Nazareth and the charlatan in question wanted him to be born in Bethlehem. None of it makes any sense, whatsoever. If there was an empty grave, no one knew what happened to after the empty grave was discovered. No one knew what Jesus said or did. Each author made up a different story, and each story grew more and more bizarre and less and less believable. The bottom line is that the Old Testament says nothing about heaven, hell or the Devil in the earliest books. The wisest man who ever lived said, point-blank, that there is no afterlife. Any verses about a possible resurrection are few and far between, and how credible are the speakers? And the New Testament is one of the most deceitful books ever written, if not THE most deceitful. Can a true religion be based on lies? by Michael R. Burch

I see many people online arguing for Jesus mythicism. However, I have also read in several places that scholars reconsider this a fringe theory. Do many mainstream scholars doubt the existence of an itinerant preacher named Jesus of Nazareth? THE CASE FOR JESUS MYTHICISM by Michael R. Burch Is there a case for Jesus mythicism — the idea that Jesus of Nazareth was entirely a myth, not a real person? Before I explore the issue, let me say that I think — not “believe” or “know,” but more of an educated guess — that there probably was an obscure Jewish rabbi that no one in power knew or cared anything about. Thus no trial before Pilate or Herod. No miracles except maybe a faith healing here and there. No walking on water, which is physically impossible. No claiming to be “god” or the “unique son of god” which would have gotten Jesus stoned to death, probably. And probably no crucifixion, since the cross was not mentioned in regard to Christianity outside the shamelessly fudged New Testament texts, until the second century AD, from what I understand. But possibly an empty grave and wild rumors of a “resurrection” that inspired the religion we now call Christianity. However, it bears noting that if there was an empty grave, the case for a “real” resurrection falls apart because it’s clear from the four gospels and the book of Acts that no one had a clue what happened to Jesus after the alleged “resurrection.” A resurrection without a resurrectee is not very impressive! Think about it. If you interacted with the resurrected God who had died for the sins of the world and was offering you salvation and the gift of eternal life in heaven, wouldn’t you remember where you saw him and what he said and did? But no one in the New Testament had a clue, so five different accounts all say radically different things. True believers do not make up sh-t about the God they truly believe in. Only charlatans trying to manipulate other people would that. However, it is possible that there was a real Jesus and rumors of an empty grave, explaining the core belief, and that the outrageous lying came later, as the cult expanded and charlatans began manipulating it for their own purposes. But again, this is just what I think, and I believe there is a very good case for Jesus mythicism. Here’s why… First, there is not a shred of testimony by any contemporary of Jesus, outside the Bible, that he actually lived. Josephus was born after the alleged death of Jesus and thus could not have been an eyewitness. Furthermore, the tiny bits Josephus allegedly “wrote” about Jesus were clearly either added entirely or heavily forged by Christian charlatans. We know this because if a religious Jew like Josephus had really believed Jesus was the Messiah, he would have written a LOT more about the most important figure, not only in Jewish history, but in the history of the world. If you were writing the history of Christianity, would you give Jesus three rushed sentences, then write a massive tome about far lesser figures like Andrew and Thomas? Of course not, and neither would Josephus dash off three sentences about someone he believed to be the Messiah. Here is what Josephus allegedly wrote: “Now, there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if it be lawful to call him a man, for he was a doer of wonderful works—a teacher of such men as receive the truth with pleasure. He drew over to him both many of the Jews, and many of the Gentiles. He was [the] Christ; and when Pilate, at the suggestion of the principal men amongst us, had condemned him to the cross, those that loved him at the first did not forsake him, for he appeared to them alive again the third day, as the divine prophets had foretold these and ten thousand other wonderful things concerning him; and the tribe of Christians, so named from him, are not extinct at this day.” The forgers were apparently cramped for space. They had no knowledge of Israel at the time of Jesus, saying he drew the Gentiles when Jesus said himself that he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel and it was Paul who drew Gentiles to Christianity after Jesus’s death. Also the Jews have no belief that the Messiah will die and be resurrected, so Josephus would not have said that. Nor do the Jews believe the prophets foretold “ten thousand wonderful things” about the Messiah. The entire passage is what Christians believe about Jesus, not what first century Jews believed about the Messiah. And “not extinct to this day” sounds like someone writing in the 2nd or 3rd century AD, after Roman attempts to get rid of Christians had failed, not something someone would write a few years after Jesus’s death. The Testimonium Flavianum is clearly the work of forgers. Does an all-powerful God need forgers to “help” him make himself known to human beings? It seems unlikely to me. Second, there is also not a shred of testimony by any eyewitness inside the Bible, that Jesus existed. We have no testimony from any of the apostles, which seems very, very odd. We don’t hear any NT author saying “Peter told me this” or “James told me that.” The apostles other than Judas all survived Jesus, and any true believer would have moved heaven and earth to get their testimonies, but we have none. Nada. Nil. Very, very odd indeed. Third, it’s beyond obvious that large parts of Jesus’s “life” were lifted directly from myths of far more ancient “saviors” like Dionysus, Horus, Krishna, Mithra, Romulus, et al. “Anything your savior can do, mine can do better!” seems to have been the modus operandi of the authors and redactors of the New Testament. Clearly mythical features of the “life” of Jesus that were plagiarized from more ancient “saviors” include: This is “been there, done that” for any number of ancient saviors. No right-thinking person can believe such copycatted nonsense, so the question becomes: Was there a real Jesus whose “resume” got padded by really bad liars who couldn’t keep their lies straight, or was Jesus always entirely mythical? While I believe there is a strong case for Jesus mythicism, I lean toward a real, entirely human and nonmagical Jesus, for primarily one reason: Mary Magdalene The only consistent thing about the entire New Testament — a book full of wild lies and wilder contradictions — is that Mary Magdalene was at the empty grave and that whatever role she played made her impossible to write out. The fact that none of the lying male chauvinist authors of the Bible were able to write out Mary Magdalene in favor of penis-equipped Peter or John makes me think it was widely known that she was the first Christian. And the most likely reason for that is that something made Mary Magdalene think Jesus was alive despite his having died. It could have been an empty grave. It could have been some sort of dream or vision. There could have been some sort of near death experience (NDE). Such things are not uncommon. I am not a Christian, but an agnostic. I don’t believe Jesus walked on water, turned water into wine, or raised the dead. I don’t think he was resurrected bodily and was walking through walls, soaring into the clouds like Superman, etc. But it’s not that unusual for people to think they have seen and/or communicated with their departed loved ones. My educated guess is that something happened that made Mary Magdalene think Jesus was still alive, even though no one else ever saw or spoke to him, requiring the authors of the four gospels and Acts to make up five incompatible lie-filled stories about what happened after the “resurrection.” It’s too bad we don’t have Mary Magdalene’s account of what happened. Burch To understand “how” Jesus turned water into wine at the wedding at Cana, we have to understand how the texts that became the New Testament were written. The gospel of John is the only gospel where the first “miracle” of Jesus was mentioned. Oddly, none of the other authors of the New Testament bothered to mention the amazing initial miracle that announced Jesus as the Messiah and a worker of wonders. Why? Why would every other author of the New Testament — all of whom were trying to convince the world that Jesus was not only the Messiah, but God incarnate, fail to mention the miracle that announced his godhood to the world? Because it never happened. The gospel of John was written after the other gospels, and long after lying about the “miracles” of Jesus had become commonplace. Why were such “miracles” made up, so frivolously and so ludicrously? Because the early Christians were in competition with other “gods” whose cults claimed they were workers of wonders. It was a race to see which cult could out-lie the others. The ancient Greeks believed the god Dionysus turned water into wine, thus Christians deemed it necessary for Jesus to turn water into wine. But it goes deeper than that, to Christians drinking the blood of Jesus at communion. Dionysus was said to turn water into wine, including a yearly miracle that took place on the fifth of January, when a spring in the temple of Dionysus would start flowing with wine. This day was called “God's Gift Day.” In The Bacchae, a story about Dionysus written by Euripides in 405 BC, wine is called the “blood of Dionysus” and drinking his blood is said to lead to immortality. Such “saviors” include but are not limited to… Thulis of Egypt came down from heaven to benefit mankind and was said to be full of grace and truth. Thulis suffered a violent death on a cross, was buried, resurrected, then ascended to heaven, where he became the judge of the dead. This was circa 1700 BC, nearly two millennia before Jesus. Romulus the founder of Rome is of particular interest because after the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD, the early Christian church recentered in Rome and that’s where the Catholic church evolved. Thus Jesus as a god or demigod would have been in competition with Romulus, the founder of Rome. The similarities of the Jesus myth to the myth of Romulus are striking and were reported by Plutarch and/or Livy: Horus of Egypt is of particular interest because Egypt and Palestine are so close to each other and are connected by myths of Joseph and Moses (an Egyptian name). Osiris was the Father of Horus and part of the triune godhead of Osiris, Isis and Horus. Krishna was born of the Virgin Devaki (“Divine One”) on December 25 in a lowly cave after being sent from heaven to earth as the human incarnation of a triune god. What is a poem on the moon in any specific language? MOON POEMS by Michael R. Burch These are poems about the moon and moonlight from various languages including Chinese, English, French, German, Indonesian, Japanese, Kurdish, Latin, Native American, Persian, Spanish, Tamil, Turkish, Ukrainian and Urdu. Quiet Night Thoughts by Li Bai aka Li Po loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Moonlight illuminates my bed as frost brightens the ground. Lifting my eyes, the moon allures. Lowering my eyes, I long for home. My interpretation of this famous poem is a bit different from the norm. The moon symbolizes love, so I imagine the moon shining on Li Bai’s bed to be suggestive, an invitation. A man might lower his eyes to avoid seeing something his wife would not approve of. This world? Moonlit dew flicked from a crane’s bill. —Eihei Dogen Kigen, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Outside my window the plums, blossoming, within their curled buds, contain the spring; the moon is reflected in the cup-like whorls of the lovely flowers I gather and twirl. —Eihei Dogen Kigen, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch The moon has long since set; the Pleiades are gone; now half the night is spent yet here I sleep alone. —Sappho, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Kin by Michael R. Burch O pale, austere moon, haughty beauty ... what do we know of love, or duty? …“The sun and lady-moon, they lave their tresses in the main, and find such cleansing in each wave, they return twice bright again.”… —excerpt from “The Fisher” by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Pausing between clouds the moon rests in the eyes of its beholders —Matsuo Basho, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Tzu Yeh (circa 400 BC) loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch I could not sleep with the full moon haunting my bed! I thought I heard―here, there, everywhere― disembodied voices calling my name! Helplessly I cried "Yes!" to the phantom air! Excerpt from “To the Moon” by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe loose translations/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Scattered, pole to starry pole, glide Cynthia's mild beams, whispering to the receptive soul whatever moonbeams mean. Bathing valley, hill and dale with her softening light, loosening from earth’s frigid chains my restless heart tonight! Over the landscape, near and far, broods darkly glowering night; yet welcoming as Friendship’s eye, she, soft!, bequeaths her light. Touched in turn by joy and pain, my startled heart responds, then floats, as Whimsy paints each scene, to soar with her, beyond... I mean Whimsy in the sense of both the Romantic Imagination and caprice. Here, I have the idea of Peter Pan flying off with Tinker Bell to Neverland. I think of you when the sun shines softly on me; also when the moon silvers each tree. —excerpt from “Near His Beloved” by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Moon Poem by Michael R. Burch I climb the mountain to inquire of the moon … the advantages of loftiness, absence, distance. Is it true that it feels no pain, or will she contradict me? Originally published by Borderless Journal (Singapore). The use of "it" and "she" is intentional, because the speaker doesn't know if the moon is impervious to pain or has consciousness. By such pale moonlight even the wisteria's fragrance seems distant. —Yosa Buson, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Leaves like crows’ shadows flirt with a lonely moon. —Kaga no Chiyo, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch In this Ordinary Swoon by Michael R. Burch In this ordinary swoon as I pass from life to death, I feel no heat from the cold, pale moon; I feel no sympathy for breath. Who I am and why I came, I do not know; nor does it matter. The end of every man’s the same and every god’s as mad as a hatter. I do not fear the letting go; I only fear the clinging on to hope when there’s no hope, although I lift my face to the blazing sun and feel the greater intensity of the wilder inferno within me. You left our house as the moon deserts night's skies, as the evening light abandons its cycle. —Mirza Ghalib, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Before you judge a man for his sins be sure to trudge many moons in his moccasins. —Native American proverb, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Oh, brilliant moon is it true that even you must fly as if you're tardy? ―Issa, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch The moon has risen once again, yet you are not here. My heart is a blazing pyre; what do I do? —Majrooh Sultanpuri, loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Dispensing Keys by Hafiz aka Hafez loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch The imbecile constructs cages for everyone he knows, while the sage (who has to duck his head whenever the moon glows) keeps dispensing keys all night long to the beautiful, rowdy, prison gang. The Lonely Earth by Kajal Ahmad loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch The pale celestial bodies never bid her "Good morning!" nor do the creative stars kiss her. Earth, where so many tender persuasions and roses lie interred, might expire for the lack of a glance, or an odor. She's a lonely dusty orb, so very lonely!, as she observes the moon's patchwork attire knowing the sun's an imposter who sears with rays he has stolen for himself and who looks down on the moon and earth like lodgers. To the boy Elis by Georg Trakl, an Austrian poet who wrote in German loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Elis, when the blackbird cries from the black forest, it announces your downfall. Your lips sip the rock-spring's blue coolness. Your brow sweats blood recalling ancient myths and dark interpretations of birds' flight. Yet you enter the night with soft footfalls; the ripe purple grapes hang suspended as you wave your arms more beautifully in the blueness. A thornbush crackles; where now are your moonlike eyes? How long, oh Elis, have you been dead? A monk dips waxed fingers into your body's hyacinth; Our silence is a black abyss from which sometimes a docile animal emerges slowly lowering its heavy lids. A black dew drips from your temples: the lost gold of vanished stars. TRANSLATOR'S NOTE: I believe that in the second stanza the blood on Elis's forehead may be a reference to the apprehensive bloody sweat of Jesus in the garden of Gethsemane. If my interpretation is correct, Elis hears the blackbird's cries, anticipates the danger represented by a harbinger of death, but elects to continue rather than turn back. From what I have been able to gather, the color blue had a special significance for Georg Trakl: it symbolized longing and perhaps a longing for death. The colors blue, purple and black may represent a progression toward death in the poem. Full Moon by Yahya Kemal Beyatli loose translation by Nurgül Yayman and Michael R. Burch You are so lovely the full moon just might delight in your rising, as curious and bright, to vanquish night. But what can a mortal man do, dear, but hope? I’ll ponder your mysteries and (hmmmm) try to cope. We both know you have every right to say no. Canción del jinete (“The Horseman’s Song” or “Song of the Rider”) by Federico Garcia Lorca loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Cordoba. Distant and lone. Black pony, big moon, olives in my saddlebag. Although my pony knows the way, I never will reach Cordoba. High plains, high winds. Black pony, blood moon. Death awaits me, watching from the towers of Cordoba. Such a long, long way! Oh my brave pony! Death awaits me before I arrive in Cordoba! Cordoba. Distant and lone. Gacela of the Dark Death by Federico Garcia Lorca loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch I want to sleep the dreamless sleep of apples far from the bustle of cemeteries. I want to sleep the dream-filled sleep of the child who longed to cut out his heart on the high seas. I don't want to hear how the corpse retains its blood, or how the putrefying mouth continues accumulating water. I don't want to be informed of the grasses’ torture sessions, nor of the moon with its serpent's snout scuttling until dawn… Kindred by Michael R. Burch Rise, pale disastrous moon! What is love, but a heightened effect of time, light and distance? Did you burn once, before you became so remote, so detached, so coldly, inhumanly lustrous, before you were able to assume the very pallor of love itself? What is the dawn now, to you or to me? We are as one, out of favor with the sun. We would exhume the white corpse of love for a last dance, and yet we will not. We will let her be, let her abide, for she is nothing now, to you or to me. If the Last Rom Dies by Mixa Kozimirenko loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch If the last Rom dies, a star would vanish above the tent, mountains and valleys moan, horses whinny in open fields, thunderclouds shroud the moon, fiddles and guitars gently weep, giants and dwarfs mourn… Song by Renée Vivien loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch When the moon weeps, illuminating flowers on the graves of the faithful, my memories creep back to you, wrapped in flightless wings. It's getting late; soon we will sleep (your eyes already half closed) steeped in the shimmering air. O, the agony of burning roses: your forehead discloses a heavy despondency, though your hair floats lightly ... In the night sky the stars burn whitely as the Goddess nightly resurrects flowers that fear the sun and die before dawn ... Undine by Renée Vivien loose translation/interpretation by Kim Cherub (an alias of Michael R. Burch) Your laughter startles, your caresses rake. Your cold kisses love the evil they do. Your eyes—blue lotuses drifting on a lake. Lilies are less pallid than your face. You move like water parting. Your hair falls in rootlike tangles. Your words like treacherous rapids rise. Your arms, flexible as reeds, strangle, Choking me like tubular river reeds. I shiver in their enlacing embrace. Drowning without an illuminating moon, I vanish without a trace, lost in a nightly swoon. "Vande Mataram" by Subramanya Bharathi, a Tamil poet loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch …Your skies are moonlit through the nightwatch’s hours while your groves emit the soft incense of flowers. Birds chirping in the trees remind us of your blessings. Venerably, we bow before you… Ehad-e-Tifli (“The Age of Infancy”) by Allama Iqbal aka Muhammad Iqbal loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch The earth and the heavens remained unknown to me, My mother's bosom was my only world. Her embraces communicated life's joys While I babbled meaningless sounds. During my infancy if someone alarmed me The clank of the door chain consoled me. At night I observed the moon, Following its flight through distant clouds. By day I pondered earth’s terrain Only to be surprised by convenient explanations. My eyes ingested light, my lips sought speech, I was curiosity incarnate. Catullus VII aka Carmina 7: “How Many Kisses” loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch You ask, Lesbia, how many kisses are enough, or more than enough, to satisfy me? As many as the Libyan sands swirling in incense-bearing Cyrene between the torrid oracle of Jove and the sacred tomb of Battiades. Or as many as the stars observing amorous men making love furtively on a moonless night. As many of your kisses are enough, and more than enough, for mad Catullus, as long as there are too many to be counted by inquisitors and by malicious-tongued bewitchers. THE WORLD'S FIRST FACE by W. S. Rendra loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Illuminated by the pale moonlight the groom carries his bride up the hill— both of them naked, both consisting of nothing but themselves… …Illuminated by the pale moonlight the groom carries his bride up the hill— both of them naked, to recreate the world's first face. If You Forget Me by Pablo Neruda loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch I need you to know one thing ... You know how it goes: if I gaze up at the glowing moon, if observe the blazing autumn's reddening branches from my window, if I touch the impalpable ash of the charred log's wrinkled body ... everything returns me to you, as if everything that exists —all aromas, sights, solids— were small boats sailing toward those isles of yours that await me… These are original poems of mine about the moon… Distances by Michael R. Burch Moonbeams on water — the reflected light of a halcyon star now drowning in night… So your memories are. Footprints on beaches now flooding with water; the small, broken ribcage of some primitive slaughter… So near, yet so far. Goddess by Michael R. Burch “What will you conceive in me?”— I asked her. But she only smiled. “Naked, I bore your child when the wolf wind howled, when the cold moon scowled . . . naked, and gladly.” “What will become of me?”— I asked her, as she absently stroked my hand. Centuries later, I understand; she whispered—“I Am.” This was the first poem to appear in the first issue of Romantics Quarterly; it has also been published by Penny Dreadful, Unlikely Stories, Underground Poets, Poetically Speaking, Poetry Life & Times and Little Brown Poetry Adrift by Michael R. Burch I helplessly loved you although I was lost in the veils of your eyes, grown blind to the cost of my ignorant folly —your unreadable rune— as leashed tides obey an indecipherable moon. Free Fall by Michael R. Burch These cloudless nights, the sky becomes a wheel where suns revolve around an axle star … Look there, and choose. Decide which moon is yours. Sink Lethe-ward, held only by a heel. Advantage. Disadvantage. Who can tell? To see is not to know, but you can feel the tug sometimes—the gravity, the shell as lustrous as damp pearl. You sink, you reel toward some draining revelation. Air— too thin to grasp, to breathe. Such pressure. Gasp. The stars invert, electric, everywhere. And so we fall, down-tumbling through night’s fissure … two beings pale, intent to fall forever around each other—fumbling at love’s tether … now separate, now distant, now together. Sunset by Michael R. Burch This poem is dedicated to my grandfather, George Edwin Hurt, who died April 4, 1998. Between the prophecies of morning and twilight’s revelations of wonder, the sky is ripped asunder. The moon lurks in the clouds, waiting, as if to plunder the dusk of its lilac iridescence, and in the bright-tentacled sunset we imagine a presence full of the fury of lost innocence. What we find within strange whorls of drifting flame, brief patterns mauling winds deform and maim, we recognize at once, but cannot name. Heat Lightening by Michael R. Burch Each night beneath the elms, we never knew which lights beyond dark hills might stall, advance, then lurch into strange headbeams tilted up like searchlights seeking contact in the distance … Quiescent unions … thoughts of bliss, of hope … long-dreamt appearances of wished-on stars … like childhood’s long-occluded, nebulous slow drift of half-formed visions … slip and bra … Wan moonlight traced your features, perilous, in danger of extinction, should your hair fall softly on my eyes, or should a kiss cause them to close, or should my fingers dare to leave off childhood for some new design of whiter lace, of flesh incarnadine. Instruction by Michael R. Burch Toss this poem aside to the filigreed and the prettified tide of sunset. Strike my name, and still it is all the same. The onset of night is in the despairing skies; each hut shuts its bright bewildered eyes. The wind sighs and my heart sighs with her— my only companion, O Lovely Drifter! Still, men are not wise. The moon appears; the arms of the wind lift her, pooling the light of her silver portent, while men, impatient, are beings of hurried and harried despair. Now willows entangle their fragrant hair. Men sleep. Cornsilk tassels the moonbright air. Deep is the sea; the stars are fair. I reap. Moon Lake by Michael R. Burch Starlit recorder of summer nights, what magic spell bewitches you? They say that all lovers love first in the dark … Is it true? Is it true? Is it true? Starry-eyed seer of all that appears and all that has appeared— What sights have you seen? What dreams have you dreamed? What rhetoric have you heard? Is love an oration, or is it a word? Have you heard? Have you heard? Have you heard? I believe I wrote this poem around age 18, during my "Romantic Period." Infinity by Michael R. Burch Have you tasted the bitterness of tears of despair? Have you watched the sun sink through such pale, balmless air that your heart sought its shell like a crab on a beach, then scuttled inside to be safe, out of reach? Might I lift you tonight from earth’s wreckage and damage on these waves gently rising to pay the moon homage? Or better, perhaps, let me say that I, too, have dreamed of infinity … windswept and blue. This is one of the first poems that made me feel like a "real" poet. I remember reading the poem and asking myself, "Did I really write that?" Many years later, I'm still glad that I wrote it, and it still makes me feel like a real poet! This is another poem that was longer and got "pared down" to its best lines. I believe I wrote it around 1976, at age 18. She Was Very Strange, and Beautiful by Michael R. Burch She was very strange, and beautiful, like a violet mist enshrouding hills before night falls when the hoot owl calls and the cricket trills and the envapored moon hangs low and full. She was very strange, in a pleasant way, as the hummingbird flies madly still, so I drank my fill of her every word. What she knew of love, she demurred to say. She was meant to leave, as the wind must blow, as the sun must set, as the rain must fall. Though she gave her all, I had nothing left … yet I smiled, bereft, in her receding glow. To Flower by Michael R. Burch When Pentheus ["grief'] went into the mountains in the garb of the baccae, his mother [Agave] and the other maenads, possessed by Dionysus, tore him apart (Euripides, Bacchae; Apollodorus 3.5.2; Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.511-733; Hyginus, Fabulae 184). The agave dies as soon as it blooms; the moonflower, or night-blooming cereus, is a desert plant of similar fate. We are not long for this earth, I know— you and I, all our petals incurled, till a night of pale brilliance, moonflower aglow. Is there love anywhere in this strange world? The Agave knows best when it's time to die and rages to life with such rapturous leaves her name means Illustrious. Each hour more high, she claws toward heaven, for, if she believes in love at all, she has left it behind to flower, to flower. When darkness falls she wilts down to meet it, where something crawls: beheaded, bewildered. And since love is blind, she never adored it, nor watches it go. Can we be as she is, moonflower aglow? In Praise of Meter by Michael R. Burch The earth is full of rhythms so precise the octave of the crystal can produce a trillion oscillations, yet not lose a second's beat. The ear needs no device to hear the unsprung rhythms of the couch drown out the mouth's; the lips can be debauched by kisses, should the heart put back its watch and find the pulse of love, and sing, devout. If moons and tides in interlocking dance obey their numbers, what's been left to chance? Should poets be more lax—their circumstance as humble as it is?—or readers wince to see their ragged numbers thin, to hear the moans of drones drown out the Chanticleer? Originally published by The Eclectic Muse, then by The Best of the Eclectic Muse 1989-2003 Finally to Burn (the Fall and Resurrection of Icarus) by Michael R. Burch Athena takes me sometimes by the hand and we go levitating through strange Dreamlands where Apollo sleeps in his dark forgetting and Passion seems like a wise bloodletting and all I remember ,upon awaking, is: to Love sometimes is like forsaking one’s Being—to glide heroically beyond thought, forsaking the here for the There and the Not. * O, finally to Burn, gravity beyond escaping! To plummet is Bliss when the blisters breaking rain down red scabs on the earth’s mudpuddle ... Feathers and wax and the watchers huddle ... Flocculent sheep, O, and innocent lambs!, I will rock me to sleep on the waves’ iambs. * To sleep's sweet relief from Love’s exhausting Dream, for the Night has Wings gentler than Moonbeams— they will flit me to Life like a huge-eyed Phoenix fluttering off to quarry the Sphinx. * Riddlemethis, riddlemethat, Rynosseross, throw out the Welcome Mat. Quixotic, I seek Love amid the tarnished rusted-out steel when to live is varnish. To Dream—that’s the thing! Aye, that Genie I’ll rub, soak by the candle, aflame in the tub. * Riddlemethis, riddlemethat, Rynosseross, throw out the Welcome Mat. Somewhither, somewhither aglitter and strange, we must moult off all knowledge or perish caged. * I am reconciled to Life somewhere beyond thought— I’ll Live the Elsewhere, I’ll Dream of the Naught. Methinks it no journey; to tarry’s a waste, so fatten the oxen; make a nice baste. I’m coming, Fool Tom, we have Somewhere to Go, though we injure noone, ourselves wildaglow. These Hallowed Halls by Michael R. Burch a young Romantic Poet mourns the passing of an age . . . I. A final stereo fades into silence and now there is seldom a murmur to trouble the slumber of these ancient halls. I stand by a window where others have watched the passage of time—alone, not untouched. And I am as they were . . . unsure . . . for the days stretch out ahead, a bewildering maze. II. Ah, faithless lover— that I had never touched your breast, nor felt the stirrings of my heart, which until that moment had peacefully slept. For now I have known the exhilaration of a heart that has vaulted the Pinnacle of Love, and the result of each such infatuation— the long freefall to earth, as the moon glides above. III. A solitary clock chimes the hour from far above the campus, but my peers, returning from their dances, heed it not. And so it is that we fail to gauge Time’s speed because He moves so unobtrusively about His task. Still, when at last we reckon His mark upon our lives, we may well be surprised at His thoroughness. IV. Ungentle maiden— when Time has etched His little lines so carelessly across your brow, perhaps I will love you less than now. And when cruel Time has stolen your youth, as He certainly shall in course, perhaps you will wish you had taken me along with my broken heart, even as He will take you with yours. V. A measureless rhythm rules the night— few have heard it, but I have shared it, and its secret is mine. To put it into words is as to extract the sweetness from honey and must be done as gently as a butterfly cleans its wings. But when it is captured, it is gone again; its usefulness is only that it lulls to sleep. VI. So sleep, my love, to the cadence of night, to the moans of the moonlit hills' bass chorus of frogs, while the deep valleys fill with the nightjar’s shrill, cryptic trills. But I will not sleep this night, nor any . . . how can I—when my dreams are always of your perfect face ringed by soft whorls of fretted lace, framed by your perfect pillowcase? VII. If I had been born when knights roamed the earth and mad kings ruled savage lands, I might have turned to the ministry, to the solitude of a monastery. But there are no monks or hermits today— theirs is a lost occupation carried on, if at all, merely for sake of tradition. For today man abhors solitude— he craves companions, song and drink, seldom seeking a quiet moment, to sit alone, by himself, to think. VIII. And so I cannot shut myself off from the rest of the world, to spend my days in philosophy and my nights in tears of self-sympathy. No, I must continue as best I can, and learn to keep my thoughts away from those glorious, uproarious moments of youth, centuries past though lost but a day. IX. Yes, I must discipline myself and adjust to these lackluster days when men display no chivalry and romance is the "old-fashioned" way. X. A single stereo flares into song and the first faint light of morning has pierced the sky's black awning once again. XI. This is a sacred place, for those who leave, leave better than they came. But those who stay, while they are here, add, with their sleepless nights and tears, quaint sprigs of ivy to the walls of these hallowed halls. I vividly remember writing the first version of “These Hallowed Halls” early my freshman year of college as I watched my peers returning from rush week parties by the light of an eerie moon.

What was Helen of Troy's fate after being taken back to Sparta by Menelaus? Did she have any more children? WHAT BECAME OF HELEN OF TROY? by Michael R. Burch The truth is that we really don’t know what happened to Helen of Troy after the fabled city fell, because there are various conflicting accounts. In “To Have Loved” rather than making up something, I imagine Helen like so many women in times of war, embracing her husband while wondering what will become of her when he dies… To Have Loved by Michael R. Burch "The face that launched a thousand ships ..." Helen, bright accompaniment, accouterment of war as sure as all the polished swords of princes groomed to lie in mausoleums all eternity ... The price of love is not so high as never to have loved once in the dark beyond foreseeing. Now, as dawn gleams pale upon small wind-fanned waves, amid white sails, ... now all that war entails becomes as small, as though receding. Paris in your arms was never yours, nor were you his at all. And should gods call in numberless strange voices, should you hear, still what would be the difference? Men must die to be remembered. Fame, the shrillest cry, leaves all the world dismembered. Hold him, lie, tell many pleasant tales of lips and thighs; enthrall him with your sweetness, till the pall and ash lie cold upon him. Is this all? You saw fear in his eyes, and now they dim with fear’s remembrance. Love, the fiercest cry, becomes gasped sighs in his once-gallant hymn of dreamed “salvation.” Still, you do not care because you have this moment, and no man can touch you as he can ... and when he’s gone there will be other men to look upon your beauty, and have done. Smile—woebegone, pale, haggard. Will the tales paint this—your final portrait? Can the stars find any strange alignments, Zodiacs, to spell, or unspell, what held beauty lacks? “To Have Loved” is a poem about the roles men and women sometimes play during times of war. Paris is no longer fully Helen's because he is being called away to battle. The calls of "fame" and "honor" can be stronger than the bonds of love. Helen feels that she is obliged to offer Paris her body and embraces until he lies dead (the "pall and ashes"). But she also feels that she has become an object, like the polished sword he carries, if he can choose it over her. In the final line "held beauty" has multiple meanings. Helen is being held physically by a man she may not see again. She is being held back from going with him because she is "only a woman." She is being held in a tower where everything will change if her husband dies. Will she have to find another man? If so, what will she have to do in order to ensure his protection? The face that famously "launched ten thousand ships" may prove to be her downfall, or it could be her salvation if she plays her cards right. This poem could, in some circumstances, perhaps help a soldier better understand his wife or lover's complex position.

The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? “Three faces have I.” — Lou Christie Why do Christian churches cling to outlandish beliefs like the Trinity, the loopy Garden of Eden fairytale, the Great Flood fairytale, and primitive witchdoctory like homosexuality being a “sin” and women being created to be subservient to men? Like any lie that needs more and more lies to support it, the Christian religion is a house of cards. Why did the doctrine of the Trinity evolve long after the death and alleged resurrection of Jesus? It was the last stage in series of lies… WHAT A LONG, STRANGE TRIP IT’S BEEN: THE EVOLUTION OF THE TRIUNE GOD by Michael R. Burch How did a pantheon of Israelite gods coalesce into one malevolent “god” who then evolved into an alleged “holy trinity”? This is how it happened, in stages… PHASE I: IN THE BEGINNING, POLYTHEISM According to Aaron Brody, a professor of Bible and archaeology at the Pacific School of Religion, the ancient Israelites were polytheists, "with only a small minority worshiping Yahweh alone before the historic events of 586 BC." It was in 586 BC that the the Jerusalem temple was destroyed and the Judean elites were exiled to Babylon. According to Brody this led to "a more universal vision of strict monotheism: one god not only for Judah, but for all the nations." In the beginning there was El, the Sky God, and his 70 sons and daughters, the Elohim, who together formed a pantheon of gods widely worshipped in ancient Mesopotamia. This odd poem invokes and merges with the anonymous medieval poem “Tom O’Bedlam’s Song” and W. H. Auden’s modernist poem “Musee des Beaux Arts,” which in turn refers to Pieter Breughel’s painting “The Fall of Icarus.” In the first stanza Icarus levitates with the help of Athena, the goddess or wisdom, through “strange dreamlands” while Apollo, the sun god, lies sleeping. In the second stanza, Apollo predictably wakes up and Icarus plummets to earth, or back to mundane reality, as in Breughel’s painting and Auden’s poem. In the third stanza the grounded Icarus can still fly, but only in flights of imagination through dreams of love. In the fourth and fifth stanzas Icarus joins Tom Rynosseross of the Bedlam poem in embracing madness by deserting “knowledge” and its cages (ivory towers, etc.). In the final stanza Icarus agrees with Tom that it is “no journey” to wherever they’re going together and also agrees with Tom that they will injure no one along the way, no matter how intensely they glow and radiate. The poem can be taken as a metaphor for the death and rebirth of Poetry, and perhaps also as a prophecy that Poetry will rise, radiate and reattain its former glory ... I AM! by Michael R. How humane must William Shakespeare have been to cover so many things that mattered in his time? WAS SHAKESPEARE ESPECIALLY HUMANE? by Michael R. Burch When I think of William Shakespeare, I think of a man who was a keen and shrewd observer of human nature. I also think of a writer who was extremely skilled in rhetoric, storytelling, plot development and character development. These attributes allowed Shakespeare to become the world’s greatest playwright, by near consensus. However, I don’t consider the Bard of Avon to have been the greatest lyric poet. I will identify some of the lyric poets I prefer after otherwise completing this answer. Shakespeare had the attributes of a great playwright, but I don’t think of him as being especially humane. Shakespeare seems to have been ambivalent about his characters, simply portraying them without judging them, as far as I can tell. That may make him a humanist of sorts, but does it make him humane? I believe there is a considerable difference. Trump may accept people as they are, including murderous despots like Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong-un, but he’s no Dalai Lama. In his sonnets, where we hear Shakespeare speaking in the first person about people he had relationships with, I detect a noticeable lack of warmth. I feel Shakespeare is being persuasive, perhaps at times manipulative, but doesn’t care deeply for the people he writes about and professes to love. For me, humaneness begins with warmth, with tenderness, and with compassion for other people. If we don’t love someone we can still empathize with them and try to understand their circumstances. I don’t detect that in Shakespeare. For me, Shakespeare’s love sonnets are more philosophical than passionate, more analytical than warm, more observational than truly caring (except when Shakespeare felt slighted). I don’t think Shakespeare rivals poets like William Blake, Robert Burns, Langston Hughes, Issa, Rilke, Sappho and Walt Whitman in humaneness. In acceptance and tolerance perhaps, but not in the depth of his feeling for humanity. An important aspect of humaneness, I believe, is a desire for human beings to be more humane. This has been a focal point of my own poetry, in poems like “Epitaph for a Palestinian Child” and “Frail Envelope of Flesh.” But in Shakespeare’s sonnets we mostly see him wanting others to be more humane to him. I believe Shakespeare was the world’s greatest playwright, for plays like Hamlet, King Lear, Macbeth, Romeo and Juliet, The Tempest, A Midsummer Night’s Dream, Henry IV Part I and Othello. And if he wrote the songs in his plays, Shakespeare was a great songwriter as well. But for me there were better lyric poets, including: I think there is a tendency to assume Shakespeare was the best at everything, due to his preeminence, the way many people assume the Beatles were the best at everything. For me, most of the Beatles’ first 66 singles, A&B sides, were pop-fizzy and the lyrics of those songs were typically not all that great: “Love Me Do,” “Please Please Me,” “She Loves You Yeah Yeah Yeah,” etc. Are those great lyrics, really? To study the difference in the shooting efficiency of the teammates of Chamberlain and Russell, I first found the league average fgp’s from 1956-1957 to 1971-1972 and determined that, on average, around the top 25 to top 30 players for fgp each season were above the league average. I then looked to see how many teammates the great centers had that were in the top 30, year-by-year. The more poor shooters a team has, the easier it is for opponents to double- and triple-team a great scorer like Wilt. What I discovered was very interesting… From 1956-1957 to 1962-1963, the Celtics usually had four players in the top 30 for fgp, with Sam Jones being amazingly consistent for a guard and ranking in the top 15 for eight consecutive years, through 1966. Bill Russell was in the top 5 when he was younger, then began to slip into the high 20s as he got older. Other players who made appearances in the top 30 included Bill Sharman, Tom Heinsohn, Frank Ramsey, Bailey Howell, Satch Sanders, Bob Cousy and John Havlicek. During this period Wilt normally had just one teammate in the top 30, and not usually in the 15, except for Al Attles twice (an underrated shooter). Two things seem obvious: (1) the Celtics didn’t just have a better defense, they also had better shooters than Wilt’s teams; and (2) there were ample opportunities to double- and triple-team Wilt because his teammates were below the league’s average fg. From 1963-1964 to 1965-1966 the gap narrowed as Bill Russell and Tom Heinsohn got older and dropped a bit in the accuracy department, but thanks to the consistency of Sam Jones the Celtics still had a 3-2 man advantage and the highest-ranked shooter other than Wilt. And while the gap was narrowing a bit, the Celtics could still gang-defend Wilt because he never had more than two primary scorers who were better than league-average shooters. Everything changed in 1966-1967 when the Philadelphia 76ers had five players in the top 22: Wilt (#1), Chet Walker (#6), Billy Cunningham (#16), Hal Greer (#17) and Al Attles (#22). So guess what happened? Wilt hit a crazy .683 from the field and the 76ers set an NBA record for wins and steamrolled to a championship. But the magic didn’t last and the following season only Hal Greer was in the top 30 besides Wilt. In 1970-1971 there were good shooters paired with Wilt on the Lakers, with five Lakers in the top 25, but the Milwaukee Bucks had one of the greatest shooting teams to date, with five players in the top 11, so there’s no surprise they won the championship with Kareem (#2), Jim McGlothlin (#4), Greg Smith (#6), Bobby Dandridge (#7) and the great Oscar Robertson (#11). In 1971-1972 the Lakers finally had the shooters to support Wilt’s interior dominance: Wilt (#1), Gail Goodrich (#18), Jim McMillian (#22), Jerry West (#27) and Happy Hairston (#38). I think the sleuthing above tells us the following: (1) The Celtics were able to win 11 championships in 13 seasons because they had a superior defense and (usually) four players in the top 30 for fgp. (2) When Wilt had shooters who could keep him from being gang-defended, he won two championships and set records for wins twice, but for most of his career he didn’t have that kind of shooting available. When he won with the Lakers in 1971-1972, his team had a mammoth .058 edge in fgp over their opponents, and they were .014 better than the league average fgp. Why didn’t the Lakers win the championship in 1970-1971? Because the Bucks were more efficient shooters, with a .006 edge over the Lakers in fgp, even though the Lakers were .015 better than the league average. Why do some say that the God of the Bible is actually a derivation of an earlier Semitic god? The birth of the love goddess Venus was similar to that of the biblical god Yahweh — in the endlessly fertile human imagination. THE BIRTH AND EVOLUTION OF THE BIBLICAL GODS by Michael R. Burch The biblical gods Yahweh/Jehovah and later Jesus and the mysterious Holy Ghost, are derivatives of several different gods and demigods, some of them Semitic and some from other areas of the world. This is how the biblical gods evolved over time… In the beginning was the supreme semitic god El, his consort Asherah, the Queen of Heaven, and his 70 sons and daughters, the Elohim. These names appear prominently throughout the Bible and we find the name of the supreme god El appearing in important names like Isra-el, Dani-el, Samu-el, and my own name, Micha-el, which means “Who is like El.” It is important to note that Elohim is obviously plural when used with plural verbs. Thus in the Genesis creation account we have the supreme god El saying to his sons and daughters the Elohim: “Let us (plural) make mankind in our (plural) own image” and we have the narrator saying, in the original text, “The gods (plural) made mankind in their (plural) own image, male and female created they (plural) them.” Once we understand the original concept, it makes perfect sense that men were created in the image of the male Elohim, while women were created in the image of the female Elohim. PHASE Ia: POLYTHEISM I will begin with polytheism prior to the creation of the Bible. The belief in gods probably began with a sense of awe, as primitive human beings observed the sun, moon, planets and stars with a sense of wonder and felt the tremendous effects of earthquakes, hurricanes and volcanoes. At times Nature seemed benevolent, but at other times Nature seemed angry, sometimes murderously angry. Nature seemed temperamental, like human beings. Thus it was natural for human beings to anthropomorphize Nature, creating human-like gods in the process. Nature in its various manifestations became the first gods: When Nature was angry, could the gods be appeased with offerings? Sometimes when offerings were made to the gods, good things happened. Thus the gods obviously liked human worship, praise and offerings. But when offerings were made and good things didn’t happen, did the gods want something more than ordinary food? Did they want enemies to be sacrificed? Or virgins? Or children? Even the king’s own son? Religion could quickly become a very bloody business. Meanwhile, witchdoctors who claimed to know how to intercede with the gods could make comfy livings without working like everyone else. When their “magic” didn’t work, they would inform the gullible that they hadn’t offered enough, or were too “sinful,” or some other claptrap. If prostitution is the oldest profession, religion is the most devious and the most profitable. PHASE Ib: POLYTHEISM PRODUCES PANTHEONS The next step in polytheism was the creation of pantheons of gods with specific pecking orders. Typically there was a supreme god like El, Zeus or Odin, then a hierarchy of more powerful and less powerful gods, followed by demigods who were half-human/half-divine, like Achilles and Heracles. In some cases rulers were seen as gods or demigods. This includes Egyptian pharaohs and Roman emperors. PHASE Ic: POLYTHEISM and the BIBLE According to Aaron Brody, a professor of Bible and archaeology at the Pacific School of Religion, the ancient Israelites were polytheists "with only a small minority worshiping Yahweh alone before the historic events of 586 BC." In that year, the Judean elite were exiled to Babylon and the Jerusalem temple was destroyed. According to Brody this led to "a more universal vision of strict monotheism: one god not only for Judah, but for all the nations." In the beginning of the Bible there was El, the Sky God, his consort (called variously Athirat, Asherah, Ashtoreth, Ashtaroth and Astarte), and his 70 sons and daughters, the Elohim, who together formed a pantheon of gods widely worshipped throughout ancient Mesopotamia. For the most part, I will use the name Asherah, since it is the name that appear frequently in the Bible. This family of gods, the Elohim, a plural term used repeatedly throughout the Bible, is why El said, “Let us [plural] create mankind in our [plural] own image.” And this is why in the following verse the narrator says, “So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.” But unless God is a hermaphrodite, El was speaking to male and female gods! Because Elohim is plural, a better translation would be: “So the Gods created human beings in their own images, in the images of the Gods they created them; male and female they created them.” This family of gods included: The ancient Israelites and Judeans adopted Yahweh as their tribal deity circa 1000 BC, but he was by no means an exclusive god. For example the Bible’s alleged wisest man, King Solomon, built altars to other gods (1 Kings 11: 5-7). Nor was Yahweh all-powerful, since other tribes had competing deities. For example, in an amusing Bible verse, Yahweh was unable to defeat plains-dwellers who had iron chariots! Yahweh had to stick to the mountains, but was also unable to defeat the Jebusites who controlled Jerusalem. Other tribes had more powerful gods, apparently. PHASE II: GET RIDDA THE CHICK! El’s wife was Asherah/Ashtoreth, so when Yahweh took over as the sole Israelite god, it made sense that his consort would be the Queen of Heaven. However, the male chauvinistic authors of the Bible decided that Yahweh’s wife, Ashtoreth, had to go. They railed at her at every possible opportunity. The authors of the Bible had Yahweh divorce his wife: The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead their dough, to make cakes to the Queen of Heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto other gods, that they may provoke me to anger. (Jeremiah 7:18) Why did Yahweh divorce his wife? It seems she had an affair with Baal! And they forsook the LORD, and served Baal and Ashtaroth. (Judges 2:13) Poor Yahweh, all the other gods ganged up on him! And the children of Israel did evil again in the sight of the LORD, and served Baalim, and Ashtaroth, and the gods of Syria, and the gods of Zidon, and the gods of Moab, and the gods of the children of Ammon, and the gods of the Philistines, and forsook the LORD, and served not him. (Judges 10:6) There were times when the Israelites “returned” to the not-so-tender affections of Yahweh… And Samuel spake unto all the house of Israel, saying, If ye do return unto the LORD with all your hearts, then put away the strange gods and Ashtaroth from among you, and prepare your hearts unto the LORD, and serve him only: and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines. Then the children of Israel did put away Baalim and Ashtaroth, and served the LORD only. (1 Samuel 7:3-4) And they cried unto the LORD, and said, We have sinned, because we have forsaken the LORD, and have served Baalim and Ashtaroth: but now deliver us out of the hand of our enemies, and we will serve thee. (1 Samuel 12:10) But Yahweh lost too many battles — those dratted iron chariots! — so the “returning” never lasted long. For instance, Yahweh was unable to defend the famous King Saul from the Philistines and his ex-wife. Thanks to the superior power of Ashtaroth, the Philistines were able to defeat Saul, kill and decapitate him, then parade his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth. That was some messy divorce! And they put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth: and they fastened his body to the wall of Bethshan. (1 Samuel 31:10) Such failures were no doubt the reason for the wisest man who ever lived, or ever will live, according to the Bible, to hedge his bets with a slightly different Trinity of gods: Ashtoreth, Milcom and Chemosh… And the high places that were before Jerusalem, which were on the right hand of the mount of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had builded for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Zidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of the Moabites, and for Milcom the abomination of the children of Ammon, did the king defile. (2 Kings 23:13) For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. (1 Kings 11:5) Yes, the wisest man who ever lived knew it was unwise to worship Yahweh only! And it wasn’t just Solomon who thought it best to hedge his bets… Because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon, and have not walked in my ways, to do that which is right in mine eyes, and to keep my statutes and my judgments, as did David his father. (1 Kings 11:33) The worship of other gods continued long after the time of Solomon. For instance, in the time of King Josiah… And the high places that were before Jerusalem, which were on the right hand of the mount of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had builded for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Zidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of the Moabites, and for Milcom the abomination of the children of Ammon, did the king defile. (2 Kings 23:13) There was never a king like the good King Josiah! Neither before nor after Josiah was there a king like him who turned to the Lord as he did—with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his strength, in accordance with all the Law of Moses. (2 Kings 23:25) But what did Josiah get for defending the honor of Yahweh with all his heart and soul? The Egyptians had far more powerful gods and Pharaoh Necho killed Josiah at Megiddo. Should he have bothered? PHASE III: MONOTHEISM, SORTA The Levite priests who copied and redacted the Hebrew Bible (the Old Testament to Christians) clumsily merged the Elohim into a single god, Yahweh, but there are many verses where the plural gods remain, such as the father god El saying to his sons and daughters the Elohim: “Let us make man in our image.” PHASE IV: THE SON OF MAN BECOMES THE SON OF GOD, SORTA According to the oldest gospel, Mark, there was no “virgin birth” and Jesus became the Messiah when he was baptized by John the Baptist. According to the author of Mark, this was sonship by adoption, not because Jesus was god from the beginning. PHASE V: THE BIG FISH GROWS The author of Matthew made a lot of sh*t, pardon my French, including the “virgin birth,” the “massacre of the innocents” and the “flight into Egypt.” Now God was actually Jesus’s father, but he was just a dime-a-dozen demigod, being half-human, like so many other demigods. PHASE VI: THE FATHER AND THE SON GET MUDDLED At some point early Christians began to argue about the nature of Jesus, and exactly how he was divine. The Holy Ghost was not doing a good job of leading Christians to the “truth” and the disputes became bitter and rancorous. There were Christians who believed Jesus was human but not divine, Christians who believed Jesus was adopted by God, Christians who believed Jesus was “of the same substance” as God but not the same person, Christians who believed God could not take human form, etc. PHASE 666: JESUS BECOMES GOD! The early Christians had no concept of a “trinity.” That concept evolved over the centuries after the death of Jesus and is impossible to find in the Bible without a lot of dubious gymnastics. But then Christianity is all about dubious mental gymnastics. The word “trinity” appears nowhere in the Bible. The concept was not made official until the First Council of Nicaea in 325 AD, after many years of debate. And even then it was pretty fuzzy. The Holy Ghost was especially delinquent in confirming its own divinity, which didn’t occur until the Council of Constantinople in 381 AD, nearly 400 years after the alleged birth of Jesus! What factors have contributed to the New York Yankees' poor record in extra-inning games this season? If my sources are correct: The two most likely reasons for such stats would be poor relief pitching and lack of clutch hitting. And from the agonized cries coming from New York newspapers and magazines, it’s more of the former than the latter. According to the New York Post, the bullpen is the “Yankees’ biggest trade deadline need.” According to Empire Sports Media, the “Yankees have a problem bubbling at the closer spot.” According to ESM, the situation is dire, with the pinstripers “desperately needing reinforcements by the trade deadline.” The Hartford Courant speculated about “How the Yankees can redesign their bullpen before and after the trade deadline.” Why all the angst? Well, for one thing the Yankees seem to be falling apart… In their latest late-inning blowup, the Yankees were one strike away from victory, when Clay Holmes gave up a two-run game-tying homer to Masataka Yoshida and Tommy Kahnle gave up the game-losing homer an inning later as the Yankees fell to the division rival Boston Red Sox 5-3. In his last five games, Holmes has given up five runs and four earned runs in five innings for a dreadful 7.20 ERA. That’s not what you want to see from your closer, obviously. And Holmes now has five blown saves midway through the 2024 season. Other than Luke Weaver and Michael Tonkin, the Yankees’ bullpen looks suddenly shaky, and two reliable relief pitchers are not enough when most starters go five or six innings on a good day. The Yankees’ bullpen had a collective 5.06 ERA in June. Pitching has been a major weakness for the Yankees of late. On June 15 the Yankees had MLB’s best record at 50-22 and the league’s best ERA at 2.88. But the bottom has dropped out since, as the Yankees lost 14 of 18 games while their pitching staff posted the majors’ worst ERA at a woeful 6.49. by Michael R. Burch

How does professional boxer Floyd Mayweather Jr. compare to Muhammad Ali in terms of bravery? In my opinion Floyd Mayweather Jr. does not begin to compare with Muhammad Ali in terms of bravery. Here’s why… First, “Money” Mayweather’s nickname tells us a lot about his priorities. On the other hand, Ali went 3 1/2 years without making any money from boxing, sacrificing millions when that was a lot of money, in order to make a principled stand against the Vietnam War and racism. There was no way the U.S. military was going to put Ali in harm’s way, so he could have taken the easy way out, but he refused to let his name be associated in any way with what he saw as a racist, unjust and needless war. And Ali proved to be correct, as former U.S. secretary of defense Robert McNamara later admitted that the infamous Domino Theory, on which the Vietnam War was predicated, was complete bullshit. The lives of every American who died in Vietnam and every person killed by Americans could have been spared. If “Money” Mayweather ever took a principled stand that cost him a penny, I am unaware of it. If I’m wrong, please correct me in the comments. Second, Ali never dodged anyone and he was fighting in the Golden Age of Heavyweights against the greatest group of boxers who ever laced on gloves: Sonny Liston (twice), Joe Frazier (three times), Big George Foreman (perhaps the most terrifying boxer of all time in his prime), Larry Holmes, Floyd Patterson (twice), Ken Norton (three times), Jerry Quarry (twice), Archie Moore, Earnie Shavers, Ernie Terrell, Jimmy Young, Ron Lyle, Cleveland Williams, Leon Spinks, et al. On the other hand, “Money” Mayweather carefully managed his career so that he was always fighting his major opponents on the way up, or on the way down, if he fought them at all. He never did fight Winky Wright or Sergio Martinez, for example, and he dodged prime Manny Pacquiao for years. “Money” Mayweather was a highly skilled boxer, but no one should mention him in the same breath with Muhammad Ali, when the subjects are courage, motivation and principle. by Michael R. Burch
